# Bridge-Notes - Version 1

The purpose of this document is to provide short, cross-topic connectors so the chatbot can build coherent answers when a question spans multiple modules. Use with slides (PDF) and glossary (DOCX). These notes do not introduce new facts: they summarize relationships already present in the course.

# 1) CT-WIP-TH: linking factory performance (Little's Law)

· Little's Law connects Work-in-Process(WIP), Throughput (TH) and Cycle Time (CT): WIP = TH × CT (steady state).   
· Station-level decomposition: CT(i) = CTq(i) + E[Ts(i)] → total CT accumulates queueing + service over the routing.   
· The bottleneck (highest utilization u or lowest capacity) caps system TH; reducing WIP without addressing the bottleneck only shortens CT transiently.   
·Raising utilization near 1 causes nonlinear CT growth; managing WIP and variability prevents CT blow-ups at high u.   
· Use VsM timelines to connect step-level processing/waiting with end-to-end CT and inventory positions.

Glossary anchors: Little's Law, Throughput (TH), Work in Process (WIP), Cycle time (CT), Botteneck, Cycle time by station, Timeline & Lead Time (VSM)

# 2) Variability → waiting (CTq) and utilization trade-offs

· Queueing delay depends on arrival and service variability (Ca², Cs2),utilization u,and mean service time E[Ts].   
· As u 个,CTq becomes very sensitive to variability; reducing SCV (CV²) can yield a capacity-equivalent benefit.   
·Natural processing-time variability can be lowered via task decomposition (e.g., Erlang-k phases).   
·Breakdowns/repairs inflate effective service time Te and its variability; availability a impacts E[Te] and thus u and CTq.   
·At line level, departure variability (c_d²) propagates downstream; in serial lines C a²(i)=C d²(i-1).

Glossary anchors: Coefficient of Variation (CV)& SCV, CTq approximation drivers (Ca², Cs², u, E[Ts]), Erlang-k approximation,Availability (a),Flow variability, Serial line (variability propagation)

# 3) Choosing a modeling formalism: Flowchart vs UML vs BPMN vs IDEFO

· Flowchart: simple control-flow with standardized symbols; good for procedures with limited decisions.

· UML: multiple views - Use Case (services), Class(structure), Sequence/Statechart/Activity (behavior).   
· BPMN: process-centric with Activities, Events, Gateways; supports concurrency, pools/lanes, data objects/stores.   
· IDEFO: function-centric (ICOM: Inputs, Controls, Outputs, Mechanisms) with hierarchical decomposition.   
· Practical rule: diagram per purpose 一 requirement capture (Use Case), execution logic (BPMN/Activitv). function decomposition (IDEFO). auick procedures (Flowchart).

Glossary anchors: Flowchart, UML (overview), BPMN (overview), BPMN core elements, Pools & Lanes, IDEFO (overview)

·Product tree/BOM defines components; precedence yields the graph of operations and feasible working seauences.   
· The OP-Resource matrix and resource graph allocate operations to workstations and schedules (Gantt).   
· In VSM, each step becomes a Process box with data (C/T,setup, uptime, VA,scrap); inventories and timelines expose waitina vs processina.

# 5) Multi-product and re-entrant flows: routing and mixtures at stations

· Re-entrant flows revisit the same workstation; from the station perspective this is equivalent to multiple ‘product tvpes'.   
·At a station,service time is a mixture over products weighted by their arrival shares → use composite mean/SCV.

Glossary anchors: Re-entrant flow system, Service-time mixture, Workload & utilization with multiple products, Composite routing matrix (P), Mean time in factory by product

# 6) Batch models: transport, setup reduction, k-at-once service

·Transport batching reduces arrival rate by k and changes inter-arrival SCV; batch forming adds (k-1)/2 · E[Td] on average.

· At receiving stations, CTq per item can match single-item flow with same u and individual SCVs.   
· Intra-batch processing adds (k-1)/2 · E[Ts] per item when processed sequentially.   
·Setup-before-batch:amortize setups R over k items (E[R]/k) but batch added formation/processing delays.   
·Batch service (k-at-once) couples batch inter-arrival/service variability with utilization u(B); choose k via CT trade-off.

Glossary anchors: Batch move (transport batching), Batch forming time, Batch queue waiting time (equivalence), Intra-batch processing delay, Batching for setup reduction, Batch service (k-at-once)

# 7) Information systems & Industry 4.O: data to decisions on the shop floor

· ERP integrates cross-functional data; MES provides real-time execution (dispatching, tracking, status) from PLC/SCADA sources.   
· PLM governs product data across lifecycle; horizontal/vertical integration enable end-to-end data flow.   
· loT/lloT and cloud platforms collect/serve data for monitoring,analytics and optimization (e.g., WIP/CT dashboards).   
· Predictive maintenance and condition monitoring reduce effective service time variability (fewer breakdowns → lower CTq).   
· Cyber-security is a prerequisite as connectivity expands the attack surface.

Glossary anchors: ERP, MES, PLM, Horizontal/Vertical integration, loT/IloT, Cloud computing, Predictive maintenance, Condition monitoring & RUL, Cyber security

# 8) Analytical models vs Discrete-Event Simulation (DES): when to use which

·Analytical'factory models'decompose lines/stations and are fast for sensitivity and design rules (u, CT, TH, WIP).   
· DES represents events (arivals, starts/ends, breakdowns) and states (queues, machines, operators) enabling what-if scenarios with complex logic and variability.   
· Verification vs Validation: build the model right vs build the right model; remove initial transient before steady-state statistics.   
· Use DES to validate scheduling rules,batching, re-entrant flows, resource sharing; use analytics for quick back-of-the-envelope checks and parameter sweeps.   
· Triangulate: DES results should be consistent with Litle's Law and queueing approximations at comparable u and variability.

Glossary anchors: Factory model (decomposition), Queueing systems (components), Verification vs Validation, Discrete Event Simulation (DES), Transient vs steady state

## Exercise 1 – Pallet Production Process

*Represent the following process with the Flow Process Chart diagram formalism.*

The considered industrial process is the manufacturing and assembly of a transport metal pallet. The pallet is made of three different parts: **metal sheet**, **profile**, and **frame**. Each part of the pallet is manufactured by a sequence of stations.

Particularly:
- Each **sheet** performs the operations of: cutting, corner cutting, and bending.
- Each **profile** performs the operations of: cutting, incision, drilling, and welding.
- Each **frame** performs the operations of: angle cutting and cup welding.

# Factory Analysis

## Key Formulas

**Little's Law:**
```
WIP = TH × CT
```

**Queue time:**
```
CTq = CT - E[Ts]
```

**Throughput (arrival rate):**
```
TH = λ = 1 / E[Ta]
```

**Cycle Time from WIP and TH:**
```
CT = WIP / λ
```

**Station capacity (single machine):**
```
capacity [jobs/min] = 1 / process_time [min]
```

**Station capacity (m identical machines in parallel):**
```
capacity [jobs/min] = m / process_time [min]
```

**Bottleneck rate:**
```
rb = min(station capacities)
```

**Raw process time:**
```
T0 = sum of process times of all workstations (one machine each)
```

**Critical WIP:**
```
W0 = rb × T0
```

**Best-case Throughput (TH_BEST):**
```
TH_BEST(w) = w / T0      if w ≤ W0
TH_BEST(w) = rb           if w > W0
```

**Best-case Cycle Time (CT_BEST):**
```
CT_BEST(w) = T0           if w ≤ W0
CT_BEST(w) = w / rb       if w > W0
```

---

## Exercise 1

**Problem:** A workstation with a single machine has a long-run average WIP of 20 jobs. The average inter-arrival time is 19 minutes, and the average queue time is 6 hours. Find the average processing time per job.

**Given:**
- WIP = 20 jobs
- E[Ta] = 19 minutes = 0.3167 hours → rounded to **0.3 hours** in solution
- CTq = 6 hours

**Solution:**

| Variable | Value | Unit |
|----------|-------|------|
| WIP | 20 | jobs |
| E[Ta] | 19 | minutes |
| E[Ta] | 0.3 | hours |
| CTq | 6 | hours |
| λ = TH = 1/E[Ta] | 3.2 | jobs/hour |
| CT = WIP / TH | 6.33 | hours |
| E[Ts] = CT – CTq | 0.33 | hours |
| E[Ts] | **20** | **min** |

**Answer:** The average processing time per job is **20 minutes**.

---

## Exercise 2

**Problem:** A bakery has WIP = 15 cakes, arrival rate = 3 cakes/hour, and average baking time = 18 minutes. Find the average time a cake spends in the queue.

**Given:**
- WIP = 15 cakes
- λ = 3 cakes/hour
- E[Ts] = 18 minutes = 0.3 hours

**Solution:**
```
CT  = WIP / λ = 15 / 3 = 5 hours
CTq = CT – E[Ts] = 5 – 0.3 = 4.7 hours
```

**Answer:** The average queue time is **4.7 hours**.

---

## Exercise 3

**Problem:** A tech support center has WIP = 10 calls, average processing time = 4 minutes, and average time in system (CT) = 1 hour. Find the average arrival rate.

**Given:**
- WIP = 10 calls
- E[Ts] = 4 minutes = 0.0667 hours
- CT = 1 hour

**Solution:**
```
λ = WIP / CT = 10 / 1 = 10 calls/hour
```

**Answer:** The average arrival rate is **10 calls/hour**.

# 1. Flow Process Chart – Example (Paper Production)

## 1.1 Purpose of the Example
This example illustrates how to represent a **manufacturing process** using the **Flow Process Chart** formalism.  
The objective is to translate a textual description into standardized symbols, making reasonable assumptions where information is missing.

> Important: when details are not explicitly stated in the text, **assumptions are allowed** and should be clearly documented near the diagram.

---

# 2. General Assumptions
- The process includes both **internal production** (company forest) and **external sourcing** (supplier).
- Transport activities are included when materials move between physically distinct locations.
- When it is unclear whether activities occur in the same location, **either solution is acceptable**.
- Time data are not provided; however, placeholders for time can be added near symbols.

---

# 3. Raw Material Supply

## 3.1 Sources of Wood
Wood is obtained from two sources:
- Company-owned forest
- External supplier

Two valid representations are possible:
1. Represent forest and supplier as **initial warehouses**
2. Start directly with **transport activities**

Both approaches are acceptable.

## 3.2 Initial Activities
- **Operation**: Cutting trees (internal activity)
- **Operation**: Receiving wood from supplier (treated as an activity for clarity)
- **Transport**: Wood conveyed via artificial channel to storage area

---

# 4. Wood Preparation Phase

## 4.1 Storage
- **Inventory**: Wood storage area

## 4.2 Chipping
- **Transport**: Wood to chipper
- **Operation**: Chipping (standard size: 1 × 2 inches)

## 4.3 Dimensional Quality Control
- **Inspection**: Chip size inspection

### 4.3.1 Flow Splitting
- Chips too large → returned to chipper
- Chips too small → removed from the process
- Conforming chips → proceed to silos

This split can be represented by:
- Multiple outgoing arrows
- Or a single inspection followed by branched flows

---

# 5. Chip Storage and Chemical Treatment

## 5.1 Storage
- **Inventory**: Chip silos

## 5.2 Boiling
- **Transport**: Chips from silos to boiling station
- **Operation**: Boiling in caustic soda and sodium sulfide

## 5.3 Fiber Separation
- **Operation**: Low-pressure discharge vat (fiber separation)

Transport between boiling and separation may be omitted if assumed to occur in the same location.

---

# 6. Fiber Processing

## 6.1 Mechanical Treatment
- **Operation**: Centrifugation
- **Operation**: Pressing

## 6.2 Bleaching
- **Operation**: Bleaching of pulp

---

# 7. Resting Phase

## 7.1 Resting Operation
- **Delay / Waiting**: Pulp resting phase

Although physically stored in a warehouse, this phase is modeled as **waiting**, because resting is an intentional process activity.

Optional:
- **Transport** to resting area
- **Inventory** symbol if storage is emphasized

---

# 8. Paper Production

## 8.1 Pulp Processing
- **Transport**: Pulp to paper machine
- **Operation**: Water removal and compression in steam-heated cylinders
- **Operation**: Drying
- **Operation**: Wrapping into large reels

## 8.2 Storage
- **Inventory**: Reel warehouse (waiting for customer orders)

---

# 9. Final Processing and Delivery

## 9.1 Order Fulfillment
- **Transport**: Reels to cutting/rewinding machine
- **Operation**: Cutting and rewinding into smaller reels

## 9.2 Delivery
- **Transport**: Final delivery to customer

The process typically ends with:
- A **transport** (delivery)
- Or a **warehouse** (finished goods storage)

---

# 10. Notes on Diagram Construction

## 10.1 Symbols Used
- Operation: circle
- Transport: arrow
- Inspection: square
- Inventory / Storage: triangle
- Delay / Waiting: delay symbol

## 10.2 Interpretation Flexibility
- Different numbers of transport activities are acceptable.
- The key requirement is **coherence with the text**.

# 1. IDEF0 – Example  
## Breakfast Distribution in a Hospital Department

## 1.1 Purpose of the Example
This example illustrates how to model a **real operational process** using the **IDEF0 formalism**, applying:
- functional decomposition,
- hierarchical consistency,
- explicit identification of inputs, outputs, controls, and resources (ICOM).

The process is modeled using **no more than two levels of detail**, to clearly demonstrate the hierarchical logic of IDEF0.

---

# 2. Process Description (Textual Summary)

Breakfast is served every morning in a hospital department.  
Breakfast consists of:
- liquid food (milk, tea, coffee),
- dry food (cookies, croissants),
- jams and sugar.

Breakfast is transported using **wheeled cabinets**:
- In the evening, cabinets are filled with dry food.
- In the morning, liquid food is heated in the kitchen and placed in thermos inside the cabinets.
- Breakfast is delivered to patients by distribution staff.
- Cabinets are transported via elevator.
- After delivery, cabinets are brought back to the kitchen and washed for reuse.

---

# 3. Level 0 Diagram – A0

## 3.1 Activity
**A0 – Breakfast Preparation and Distribution**

This diagram represents the **entire process** as a single macro-activity.

### Inputs
- Dry food  
- Liquid food  
- Jams  
- Sugar  

### Outputs
- Breakfast served to patients  
- Clean cabinets  

### Controls
- Preparation instructions  
- Distribution instructions  
- Washing instructions  

### Resources (Mechanisms)
- Cabinets  
- Hospital staff  
- Elevator  
- Dishwasher  
- Kitchen tools  

> Note: Some controls are not explicitly mentioned in the text but are **reasonably assumed**, as allowed in IDEF0 modeling.

---

# 4. Level 1 Diagram – Decomposition of A0

## 4.1 Expanded Activities
Activity **A0** is decomposed into three sub-activities:

- **A1 – Food Preparation**
- **A2 – Breakfast Distribution**
- **A3 – Cabinet Washing**

---

## 4.2 Activity A1 – Food Preparation

### Inputs
- Dry food  
- Liquid food  
- Jams  
- Sugar  

### Output
- Cabinets filled with breakfast  

### Controls
- Preparation instructions  

### Resources
- Preparation staff  
- Cabinets  
- Kitchen tools  

---

## 4.3 Activity A2 – Breakfast Distribution

### Input
- Cabinets filled with breakfast  

### Outputs
- Breakfast served to patients  
- Cabinets to be cleaned  

### Controls
- Distribution instructions  

### Resources
- Distribution staff  
- Elevator  

---

## 4.4 Activity A3 – Cabinet Washing

### Input
- Cabinets to be cleaned  

### Output
- Clean cabinets  

### Controls
- Washing instructions  

### Resources
- Washing staff  
- Dishwasher  

---

# 5. Level 2 Diagram – Decomposition of A1 (Food Preparation)

## 5.1 Expanded Activities
Activity **A1 – Food Preparation** is further decomposed into:

- **A1.1 – Dry Food Preparation**
- **A1.2 – Liquid Food Preparation**

---

## 5.2 Activity A1.1 – Dry Food Preparation

### Inputs
- Dry food  
- Jams  
- Sugar  

### Output
- Cabinets with dry food  

### Controls
- Dry food preparation instructions  

### Resources
- Preparation staff  
- Cabinets  

---

## 5.3 Activity A1.2 – Liquid Food Preparation

### Inputs
- Liquid food  
- Cabinets with dry food  

### Output
- Cabinets with breakfast  

### Controls
- Liquid food preparation instructions  

### Resources
- Preparation staff  
- Kitchen tools  

---

# 6. Consistency Checks Between Levels

IDEF0 requires **strict consistency** across hierarchical levels:

- All inputs of A0 must appear as inputs in at least one lower-level activity.
- All outputs generated at lower levels must be reflected in higher-level diagrams.
- Resources and controls must remain coherent across decompositions.

Example:
- *Clean cabinets* appear as an output of A3 and must therefore be included as an output of A0.

---

# 7. Modeling Notes

- Temporal order can be represented by:
  - output → input connections, or
  - output → control connections.

# 1. IDEF0 – Theory

## 1.1 Introduction
IDEF0 is the last formalism introduced in this course.  
It belongs to the **IDEF family** of diagrams, developed within the **ICAM (Integrated Computer Aided Manufacturing)** project.

Different IDEF formalisms exist (IDEF0, IDEF1, IDEF1X, IDEF2, etc.), each designed for specific purposes.  
This section focuses exclusively on **IDEF0**, which is used to build **functional models** of organizations or systems.

---

# 2. Purpose of IDEF0

IDEF0 is used to:
- represent **activities/functions** of a system,
- specify **constraints and controls** between activities,
- describe systems through a **hierarchical decomposition**,
- support functional understanding rather than detailed sequencing.

Compared to previous formalisms, IDEF0 introduces new conceptual elements:
- **controls**
- **resources (mechanisms)**

---

# 3. Key Characteristics

## 3.1 Simple Graphical Language
IDEF0 uses only:
- **boxes** → activities
- **arrows** → relationships

The expressive power comes from the **position** of arrows, not from different symbols.

## 3.2 Textual Emphasis
Each diagram includes:
- a title,
- an identification code (node),
- labeled activities and flows.

## 3.3 Hierarchical Structure
IDEF0 models are **multi-level**:
- high-level diagrams show general functions,
- lower-level diagrams refine activities into more detailed sub-functions.

The model is not a single diagram, but a **set of interconnected diagrams**.

---

# 4. Hierarchical Decomposition Logic

## 4.1 Top-Level Diagram (A0)
- Represents the entire system as **one single activity**.
- This activity is labeled **A0**.

## 4.2 Lower-Level Diagrams
- The activity A0 is decomposed into activities A1, A2, A3, …
- Each of these activities can be further decomposed:
  - A1 → A11, A12, A13
  - A4 → A41, A42, A43

Each diagram explicitly references its **parent activity**, ensuring traceability.

---

# 5. Activity Representation

## 5.1 Activity Box
- Represents a function or activity.
- Labeled with a verb or short description.
- Identified by a unique number in the lower-right corner.

### Constraint
- A maximum of **six activities per diagram** is allowed.
- If more are needed, further decomposition is required.

---

# 6. Arrow Semantics (ICOM Framework)

Each activity is connected by **four types of arrows**, depending on their position.

## 6.1 Input (Left)
- Enters from the **left side**.
- Represents what is **consumed or transformed** by the activity.
- Inputs are modified by the activity.

## 6.2 Output (Right)
- Exits from the **right side**.
- Represents the **result** produced by the activity.

## 6.3 Control (Top)
- Enters from the **top**.
- Represents constraints, rules, or documents.
- Controls are **not consumed**.
- Examples:
  - manuals,
  - production plans,
  - customer requirements.

## 6.4 Resource / Mechanism (Bottom)
- Enters from the **bottom**.
- Represents resources that enable the activity:
  - machines,
  - tools,
  - people,
  - departments.
- Resources are not consumed, only their **time** is used.

---

# 7. Input vs Control: Key Concept

- **Input**: transformed by the activity and becomes part of the output.
- **Control**: consulted but not modified.

Example:
- A work plan:
  - input for a *design* activity (it is modified),
  - control for a *production* activity (it is only consulted).

---

# 8. Parallel Activities

Parallel execution can be represented by:
- connecting the **output** of one activity to the **controls** of multiple activities,
- or by splitting outputs into multiple flows.

This indicates that activities can start independently once a prerequisite output is available.

---

# 9. Examples of Activity Relationships

## 9.1 Sequential Physical Processing
- Drilling → Polishing
- Output of drilling (drilled plate) becomes input of polishing.
- Same control (work cycle) can apply to both activities.

## 9.2 Design vs Production
- Design activity outputs a **work plan**.
- Production activity uses:
  - raw materials as input,
  - work plan as control,
  - machines and operators as resources.

---

# 10. Representing Alternatives (No Decision Symbol)

IDEF0 does **not** include explicit decision symbols.

Alternative outcomes are represented by:
- multiple outputs exiting the same activity.

Example:
- Book received:
  - correct → cataloging activity,
  - incorrect → return to vendor.

The branching is implicit in the outputs.

---

# 11. Modeling Complex Systems

IDEF0 diagrams can include:
- multiple activities,
- several interacting documents,
- departments modeled as resources,
- documents flowing as inputs, outputs, or controls.

The decomposition logic keeps diagrams readable despite complexity.

---

# 12. Advantages of IDEF0

- Clear functional representation.
- Easy to understand even for non-experts.
- Strong support for hierarchical reasoning.
- Useful for:
  - system understanding,
  - responsibility allocation,
  - cost analysis (costs can be aggregated bottom-up).

---

# 13. Key Takeaway
IDEF0 is a **functional modeling formalism** focused on:
- what activities do,
- what they need,
- what constrains them,
- and what they produce.

Its hierarchical nature makes it especially effective for analyzing complex systems at multiple levels of abstraction.

# 1. Introduzione: perché servono i formalismi nel process modeling

## 1.1 Problema di fondo: comunicazione tra persone con background diversi
Nelle aziende, molte persone collaborano su processi e sistemi con linguaggi, esperienze e modelli mentali diversi. Descrivere un processo solo in forma narrativa può generare ambiguità interpretative. I formalismi servono a fornire un linguaggio condiviso e non ambiguo per la rappresentazione dei processi.

## 1.2 Metafora dello “swing”
La metafora dello swing evidenzia come ogni attore coinvolto in un progetto possa interpretare in modo diverso lo stesso requisito. Il risultato finale rischia quindi di non corrispondere alle reali esigenze dell’utente finale. L’uso di formalismi standard riduce tali fraintendimenti.

# 2. Product Lifecycle Management (PLM)

## 2.1 Definizione
Il Product Lifecycle Management descrive l’intero ciclo di vita di un prodotto, che include pianificazione, sviluppo, produzione, supporto e fine vita. Il ciclo è spesso circolare, poiché materiali e componenti possono essere riutilizzati.

## 2.2 Implicazioni per il process modeling
In ogni fase del PLM esistono processi che devono essere descritti e analizzati. La scelta del formalismo dipende dal tipo di processo e dal livello di dettaglio richiesto.

# 3. Definizione di processo
Un processo è un insieme di attività collegate che trasformano input in output. La corretta rappresentazione richiede un equilibrio tra visione d’insieme e dettaglio operativo.

# 4. Tipologie di processi
I processi possono essere classificati in information processes, physical processes e functional processes. A ciascuna categoria corrispondono formalismi più o meno adatti.

# 5. Formalismi per Information Processes

## 5.1 Flowchart
Il flowchart rappresenta in modo semplice la sequenza delle attività e le decisioni. Utilizza simboli standard come attività, decisioni e flussi.

## 5.2 UML Activity Diagram
Gli UML Activity Diagram estendono i flowchart introducendo il concetto di parallelismo tramite fork e join, permettendo una rappresentazione più espressiva.

## 5.3 BPMN
La Business Process Model and Notation offre una notazione più ricca, includendo messaggi, eventi e gateway complessi. È particolarmente adatta alla modellazione di processi di business strutturati.

# 6. Formalismi per Physical Processes

## 6.1 Flow Process Chart
Il Flow Process Chart è utilizzato per rappresentare flussi materiali e produttivi. Si basa su cinque simboli principali: operation, transport, delay, inventory e inspection.

## 6.2 Utilizzo As-Is e To-Be
Questo formalismo consente di descrivere lo stato attuale del processo e di confrontarlo con uno stato futuro migliorato, supportando l’analisi delle inefficienze.

# 7. Esempio: Cookie Factory
L’esempio della cookie factory mostra come il Flow Process Chart permetta di individuare punti critici del processo produttivo, come elevati tassi di scarto, e di ipotizzare interventi di miglioramento.

# 8. Conclusione
I formalismi di process modeling sono strumenti fondamentali per garantire chiarezza, coerenza e condivisione nella descrizione dei processi. La scelta del formalismo corretto dipende dal contesto applicativo e dagli obiettivi dell’analisi.

- First welding: **30 s**
- Second welding: **30 s**
- Assembly: **195 s**

---

# 9. Performance Indicators

## 9.1 Total Lead Time
- **Total production lead time:** ≈ **48 days**

## 9.2 Total Value‑Added Time
- Sum of processing times only (seconds)
- Negligible compared to total lead time

---

# 10. Modeling Notes and Assumptions
- Parallel processes use the **maximum processing time** in the timeline.
- Outsourced processes are treated as **non‑value‑added**.
- Inventories may be merged or separated depending on interpretation.
- Assumptions are acceptable if explicitly stated.

---

# 11. Key Takeaway
This exercise shows how Value Stream Mapping:
- reveals the dominance of non‑value‑added time,
- supports comparison between current and future states,
- provides a structured basis for Lean improvement decisions.

# 1. Value Stream Mapping (VSM) – Theory

## 1.1 Introduction
Value Stream Mapping (VSM) is the second formalism introduced for representing **material processes**.  
Although it primarily focuses on material flows, it also allows the representation of **high-level information flows** between:
- the company,
- its suppliers,
- its customers,
- and internal production control.

VSM was introduced in the 1980s by Japanese engineers working at **Toyota** and is a core tool of **Lean Manufacturing**.

---

# 2. Lean Philosophy Context

## 2.1 Lean Manufacturing
Lean Manufacturing is a production philosophy aimed at:
- reducing waste,
- eliminating non-value-added activities,
- improving overall process efficiency.

## 2.2 Role of Value Stream Mapping
Value Stream Mapping is a **diagnostic tool** used to:
- distinguish value-added vs non-value-added activities,
- visualize the entire production process at a high level,
- identify improvement opportunities.

---

# 3. Purpose of Value Stream Mapping

VSM is used to:
- represent the **current state** of a production system,
- analyze value-added and non-value-added activities,
- design and compare a **future state** with improved performance.

This logic is analogous to the *As-Is* and *To-Be* comparison previously introduced with the Flow Process Chart.

---

# 4. Structure of a Value Stream Mapping Diagram

A Value Stream Mapping diagram is divided into **three main sections**:

## 4.1 Central Section – Material Flow
- Represents the flow of materials inside the company.
- Starts from raw material arrival and ends with delivery to the customer.
- Includes only **technological processes** (e.g. cutting, welding, milling).
- Shows inventory accumulation points.

## 4.2 Upper Section – Information Flow
- Represents high-level information exchanges.
- Includes:
  - orders,
  - forecasts,
  - production planning and scheduling.
- Does not describe detailed information processes (other formalisms are used for that).

## 4.3 Lower Section – Timeline
- Represents time consumption across the process.
- Divided into:
  - **value-added time** (processing),
  - **non-value-added time** (waiting, inventory, transport).
- Used to compute total production lead time and total value-added time.

---

# 5. Key Characteristics of VSM

## 5.1 High-Level Representation
- Shows the whole process without detailing individual tasks.
- Complements analytical and quantitative models used later.

## 5.2 Waste Identification
- Helps identify where waste occurs.
- Does not directly identify causes, but highlights critical areas.

## 5.3 Common Language
- Provides a shared representation of production processes.
- Widely used in manufacturing and logistics contexts.

## 5.4 Link Between Material and Information Flows
- One of the few formalisms that explicitly connects material and information flows.

## 5.5 Qualitative but Time-Aware
- Mainly qualitative.
- Includes time information sufficient to compute lead times and efficiency indicators.

---

# 6. Main Symbols in Value Stream Mapping

## 6.1 External Entities (Supplier / Customer)
- Represented by an external factory symbol.
- Used for suppliers and customers.

### Data Box (External)
Contains information such as:
- order frequency,
- delivery frequency,
- lot size,
- material characteristics.

---

## 6.2 Process
- Represented by a rectangular box.
- Refers to **technological processes**, not entire business processes.

### Data Box (Process)
Includes:
- **Cycle Time (CT)**: processing time only (not waiting or setup).
- **Changeover Time (CO)**: setup time.
- **Uptime**: percentage of time the machine is operational.
- **Shifts / operator availability**.
- **Number of operators** (if manual activation is required).

Note:
In VSM, *cycle time* means only **effective processing time**, not total lead time.

---

## 6.3 Operators
- Represented by a specific operator icon.
- Indicates manual operation of the process.
- The number of operators is specified.

---

## 6.4 Inventory
- Represented by a triangle.
- Indicates accumulation points (buffers).
- Usually placed before processes.

Inventory data can be expressed as:
- average number of items,
- or average waiting time.

# 7. Push vs Pull Systems

## 7.1 Push System

- This course focuses mainly on push systems.

## 7.2 Pull System

- Represented with different symbols (not covered here).

# 8. Information Flow Representation

## 8.1 Manual Information Flow
- Represented by a straight arrow.

## 8.2 Electronic Information Flow

Each arrow is labeled with the type of information exchanged
(e.g. monthly orders, weekly scheduling).

---

# 9. Timeline Interpretation

## 9.1 Structure
- Lower part: **value-added time**.
- Upper part: **non-value-added time**.

## 9.2 Interpretation
- Waiting, transport, and inventory times are non-value-added.
- Processing times are value-added.

## 9.3 Performance Insight
- Often, total lead time is dominated by non-value-added time.
- This highlights improvement potential.

Example:
- Total production time: 14 days.
- Total value-added time: ~500 seconds.

---

# 10. Method to Build a Value Stream Map

1. Identify technological processes.
2. Add suppliers and customers with data boxes.
3. Define material flow and inventories.
4. Specify transport modes and frequencies.
5. Insert the timeline and compute times.
6. Add information flows.
7. Analyze current state.
8. Design and compare future state.

---

# 11. Key Takeaway
Value Stream Mapping is a powerful Lean tool that:
- visualizes the entire production system,
- highlights inefficiencies,
- links material and information flows,
- supports structured process improvement.

# 2.3 Critical Parameters of Production Lines

## 2.3.1 Introduction
This section introduces the **critical parameters** used to analyze the performance of production lines.
These parameters allow us to:
- determine the **best achievable performance** of a system,
- compare optimal conditions with actual factory behavior,
- identify inefficiencies and improvement potential.

The analysis builds on the relationships between **WIP, throughput, and cycle time**.

---

# 2.3.2 Definition of Critical Parameters

Three critical parameters characterize a production line:

## Bottleneck Rate (Rᵦ)
- Defined as the **throughput of the bottleneck workstation**.
- The bottleneck is the workstation with the **lowest capacity**.
- Rᵦ represents the **maximum achievable throughput** of the line.

---

## Raw Process Time (T₀)
- Defined as the **sum of the average processing times** of all workstations.
- Represents the **minimum possible cycle time**.
- No job can exit the system faster than T₀.

---

## Critical WIP (W₀)
- Defined as:
```
W₀ = Rᵦ · T₀
```
- Represents the minimum WIP level required to achieve:
  - maximum throughput,
  - minimum cycle time.

---

# 2.3.3 Example 1 – Balanced Production Line

### System Description
- 4 machines in series
- Each machine has:
  - processing time = 2 hours
  - capacity = 1 / 2 = 0.5 jobs/hour
- No failures, no scrap, immediate transfer

### Critical Parameters
- Bottleneck rate:
```
Rᵦ = 0.5 jobs/hour
```
- Raw process time:
```
T₀ = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 hours
```
- Critical WIP:
```
W₀ = 0.5 · 8 = 4 jobs
```

This is a **balanced line**, since all machines have the same capacity.

---

# 2.3.4 Example 2 – Unbalanced Line with Parallel Machines

### System Description
Four workstations in series:
- WS1: 1 machine, 2 h
- WS2: 2 machines, 5 h
- WS3: 6 machines, 10 h
- WS4: 2 machines, 3 h

### Workstation Capacities
Capacity of each workstation is the **sum of machine capacities**:
- WS1: 0.5 jobs/h
- WS2: 0.4 jobs/h
- WS3: 0.6 jobs/h
- WS4: 0.67 jobs/h

### Critical Parameters
- Bottleneck: WS2
```
Rᵦ = 0.4 jobs/hour
```
- Raw process time:
```
T₀ = 2 + 5 + 10 + 3 = 20 hours
```
- Critical WIP:
```
W₀ = 0.4 · 20 = 8 jobs
```

---

# 2.3.5 Industrial Example – Performance Comparison

Given:
- Bottleneck rate: 114 parts/hour
- Raw process time: 33.9 hours
- Critical WIP:
```
W₀ ≈ 3869 units
```

Actual performance:
- Throughput: 71.8 parts/hour
- WIP: 47,600 units
- Cycle time: 663 hours

### Interpretation
- Throughput ≈ 63% of maximum
- WIP ≈ 12 × critical WIP
- Cycle time ≈ 24 × raw process time

The system performs **far from optimal conditions**.

# 2.3.6 Relationship Between WIP, CT, and TH

Let:
- W = WIP level

Then:

### Cycle Time
```
CT(W) = T₀            if W ≤ W₀
CT(W) = W / Rᵦ        if W > W₀
```

### Throughput
```
TH(W) = W / T₀        if W ≤ W₀
TH(W) = Rᵦ            if W > W₀
```

---

# 2.3.7 Interpretation of the Curves

- For W ≤ W₀:
  - Throughput increases linearly
  - Cycle time remains minimal

- For W > W₀:
  - Throughput saturates at Rᵦ
  - Cycle time increases linearly with W

This region corresponds to **congestion**.

---

# 2.3.8 Exam-Style Exercise (Solved)

### Given
Three workstations in series with processing times:
- 3 min
- 2 min
- 4 min

### Solution
- Capacities:
  - WS1: 0.33 jobs/min
  - WS2: 0.5 jobs/min
  - WS3: 0.25 jobs/min
- Bottleneck:
```
Rᵦ = 0.25 jobs/min
```
- Raw process time:
```
T₀ = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 min
```
- Critical WIP:
```
W₀ = 0.25 · 9 = 4.5 jobs
```

### Behavior for W > W₀
- Throughput remains constant at Rᵦ
- Cycle time increases as W / Rᵦ

---

# 2.3.9 Key Takeaways
- Critical parameters define **optimal system performance**.
- Bottleneck determines maximum throughput.
- Excess WIP increases cycle time without increasing throughput.
- Comparing actual vs critical values reveals inefficiencies.

# 2.1 Introduction to Production System Modeling  
## Little’s Law and Exercises

## 2.1.1 Course Context and Objectives
This section introduces the **analysis and modeling of production systems**.  
It corresponds to **Chapter 2** of the reference textbook and defines the analytical framework used throughout the course.

The adopted approach is **analytical and hierarchical**:
- start from simple systems,
- derive fundamental relationships between KPIs,
- progressively extend the models to more complex systems.

---

# 2.1.2 Modeling Approach

The course follows a **bottom-up strategy**:
1. Single workstation (single machine)
2. Production line (series of workstations)
3. Networks with merging and splitting flows
4. Multiple product types
5. Batch arrivals

Each model is an **approximation** of reality:
- not all real-world elements are modeled,
- operators, transport systems, and detailed behaviors may be abstracted,
- assumptions must be justified by the analysis objectives.

---

# 2.1.3 System Boundaries

The analysis focuses on the **factory system only**:
- jobs arrive at the factory with given parameters,
- jobs follow a routing inside the factory,
- completed jobs exit the system (delivery or storage not analyzed further).

---

# 2.1.4 Basic Definitions

## Jobs
The terms *job*, *item*, and *order* are used interchangeably to indicate a physical entity entering the production system.

## Factory
A factory is composed of multiple **workstations**.

## Workstation
A workstation is a set of **identical machines or operators**:
- same processing parameters,
- parallel operation,
- identical processing time distributions.

## Queue
A physical or logical place where jobs wait when machines are busy.

## Routing
The ordered sequence of workstations visited by a job.

Different product types may follow **different routings** within the same factory.

---

# 2.1.5 Arrival Process

Jobs may arrive:
- individually,
- in batches.

Arrival is characterized by:
- average arrival rate,
- average inter-arrival time,
- probability distribution (often exponential).

These are **input parameters** of the model.

---

# 2.1.6 Processing Times

Processing times:
- are not deterministic,
- follow probability distributions,
- are characterized by mean value and variability.

---

# 2.1.7 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)

## Cycle Time (CT)
The **cycle time** is the time a job spends inside the system.

Terminology note:
- in Value Stream Mapping this quantity is often called *lead time*,
- in queueing theory and analytical models it is called *cycle time*.

Two notions:
- real cycle time: directly measured in the plant,
- planned cycle time: conservative estimate used for planning and scheduling.

### System vs Workstation Cycle Time
- CTᵢ: cycle time at workstation *i*
- CTₛ: total cycle time of the system

At workstation level:
```
CTᵢ = CTQᵢ + E[TSᵢ]
```

---

## Work In Process (WIP)
WIP is the **average number of jobs inside the system**:
- jobs being processed,
- jobs waiting in queues.

---

## Throughput (TH)
Throughput is the **rate of completed jobs** leaving the system:
- jobs per hour,
- jobs per day.

In steady state:
```
TH = arrival rate
```

---

# 2.1.8 Steady-State Assumption

Performance measures are evaluated in **steady state**:
- after initial transient effects disappear,
- independent of initial system conditions.

Instantaneous values fluctuate due to variability,  
but **average values converge** to steady-state limits.

Define for job *i*:
- arrival time: aᵢ
- departure time: dᵢ

Define:
- A(t): cumulative arrival function
- D(t): cumulative departure function

The number of jobs in the system at time *t* is:
```
N(t) = A(t) − D(t)
```

---

# 2.1.10 Average Cycle Time

For a time interval [a, b]:

```
CT = (1 / Nₐᵦ) · Σ (dᵢ − aᵢ)
```

---

# 2.1.11 Average WIP

Average WIP over [a, b]:

```
WIP = (1 / (b − a)) · ∫ N(t) dt
```

---

# 2.1.12 Little’s Law

```
WIP = TH · CT
```

Equivalent form:
```
WIP = λ · CT
```

---

# 2.1.13 Exercise 1

**Given:**
- WIP = 25 jobs  
- λ = 4 jobs/hour  
- E[TS] = 14.5 minutes  

**Solution:**
- CT = 25 / 4 = 6.25 hours  
- E[TS] = 0.24 hours  
- CTQ = 6.01 hours

**Given:**
- λ = 10 jobs/day = 0.417 jobs/hour  
- CT₁ = 4.2 hours  
- CT₂ = 5.3 hours  

**Solution:**
- WIP = λ · (CT₁ + CT₂) = 3.96 jobs  

---

# 2.1.15 Key Takeaways
- Steady-state averages are central.
- Little’s Law links WIP, CT, and TH.
- Valid at all system levels.

# 2.2 Penny Fab Model  
## Single Workstation and Factory-Level Analysis

## 2.2.1 Purpose of the Model
The **Penny Fab Model** is a didactic example used to introduce:
- analytical modeling of production systems,
- performance evaluation using **Little’s Law**,
- the impact of variability and system boundaries.

---

# 2.2.2 Modeling Philosophy
The analytical approach:
- decomposes the factory into simple components,
- models each component separately,
- recomposes the system to analyze global behavior.

This is an approximation of reality and abstracts from operators and transport systems.

---

# 2.2.3 System Boundaries
The analysis focuses only on the factory:
- jobs arrive with known parameters,
- jobs follow a routing,
- completed jobs exit the system.

---

# 2.2.4 Core Definitions

## Workstation
A workstation is a set of identical machines or operators working in parallel.

## Queue
Jobs wait in a queue when machines are busy.

## Routing
The ordered sequence of workstations visited by a job.

---

# 2.2.5 Arrival Process
Jobs may arrive individually or in batches.
Arrival is characterized by the arrival rate λ and its distribution.

---

# 2.2.6 Processing Times
Processing times are random variables with known mean and variability.

---

# 2.2.7 Performance Measures

### Cycle Time (CT)
```
CT = CTQ + E[TS]
```

### Work In Process (WIP)
Average number of jobs inside the system.

### Throughput (TH)
Completed jobs per unit of time.
In steady state:
```
TH = λ
```

---

# 2.2.8 Little’s Law
```
WIP = TH · CT
```

---

# 2.2.9 Key Insights
- Variability generates waiting.
- Waiting dominates cycle time.
- Little’s Law links all KPIs.

---

# 2.2.10 Key Takeaway
The Penny Fab Model shows how simplified analytical models provide deep insight into production system behavior.
